title: The Big Four Are Now Hiring More AI Engineers Than Auditors. For India's Tech Workforce, That Changes Everything
excerpt: Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC posted 3.5 times more AI roles than audit positions last year — and the ripple effects are already reaching Bengaluru and Hyderabad
body:
For decades, the Big Four accounting and consulting firms ran on a simple formula: hire vast numbers of junior accountants, grind them through compliance reviews and documentation checks, and promote a small fraction into the lucrative advisory and partner tiers above. That model built Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC into global consulting empires. Now it is being quietly dismantled by the same firms that profited from it.

## The Numbers

According to a Financial Times analysis of more than 50,000 job listings, AI-related roles made up nearly 7 per cent of Big Four postings in 2025 — compared to less than 2 per cent in 2022 when OpenAI's ChatGPT launched. Traditional auditing roles, the bedrock of the entire industry, accounted for less than 3 per cent. That is a 3.5-to-1 ratio in favour of AI, and the gap is widening.

KPMG advertised for managers experienced in chatbot prompt engineering and AI-agent automation. EY sought staff capable of helping tax clients adopt generative AI systems. PwC's global chair Mohamed Kande admitted the firm was struggling to hire "hundreds and hundreds" of AI engineers because demand had become so intense across the technology sector.

## Why It Matters for India

India is the Big Four's largest talent pool outside the United States. Deloitte India alone employs over 100,000 people. EY's India operations are the firm's second-largest globally. The shift from traditional audit hiring to AI recruitment is not an abstract Western trend — it is already reshaping hiring pipelines in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Gurugram.

For Indian engineering graduates, the implications are immediate. The traditional path — a commerce degree, a CA qualification, an entry-level Big Four audit role — is no longer the only route into these firms, and arguably no longer the most valued one. Data scientists, machine learning engineers and AI integration specialists are now competing for the same headcount budgets that once went exclusively to chartered accountants.

The firms are also increasingly building their AI capabilities in India rather than merely serving Western clients from Indian offices. Deloitte's AI Centre of Excellence in Hyderabad, EY's innovation hub in Bengaluru, and PwC's digital acceleration centres across multiple Indian cities are all expanding.

## The Pyramid Problem

The Big Four's traditional business model was built on a pyramid: thousands of junior staff performing repetitive, structured tasks at the base, with progressively fewer — and progressively more profitable — senior managers and partners at the top. AI is attacking the base of that pyramid.

Financial record scanning, anomaly detection, compliance document review, tax calculation and basic audit testing — the tasks that occupied thousands of entry-level professionals — are precisely the kind of structured, repetitive processes that AI handles efficiently. The firms are not eliminating audit entirely; large companies still want human sign-off on accounts, regulatory filings and risk assessments. But the volume of junior staff needed to support that work is shrinking.

For junior accountants who accepted years of demanding, repetitive work as the price of admission to a lucrative advisory career, the calculus is changing. Some of the routine tasks that filled those early years are the first to be automated.

## The Diaspora Angle

For Indian professionals working at Big Four offices in the US, UK and Middle East — many on work visas — the hiring shift creates both opportunity and anxiety. Those with AI and data science skills are in unprecedented demand. Those in traditional audit roles face a more uncertain trajectory.

The timing coincides with the proposed 30 per cent increase in H-1B minimum wages in the United States, which would raise the entry-level salary floor for visa holders to nearly $98,000. If the Big Four are simultaneously reducing traditional junior headcount and raising the bar for the technical skills they recruit, the pool of Indian professionals who qualify for visa-sponsored Big Four positions in the US could narrow significantly.

Conversely, the firms' expansion of AI centres in India itself may accelerate — offering competitive salaries without the visa complications, and giving Indian engineers access to global projects from domestic offices.

## What Comes Next

The Big Four cannot abandon audit; it remains the gateway to the corporate relationships that feed their far more profitable consulting divisions. But the workforce that supports audit is being reconstituted around automation, with fewer humans doing more valuable work alongside AI systems.

For India's massive pipeline of accounting and engineering graduates, the message is clear: the firms that once hired armies of CAs now want hybrid professionals who understand financial systems and can work comfortably with machine learning tools. The pyramid is not collapsing. It is being rebuilt with different materials.
